newsitem.title: USA: Maine gov wants cigarettes to pay for tax relief.
newsitem.headline: Maine gov wants cigarettes to pay for tax relief.

text.p: Maine Gov. Angus King on Tuesday said he wanted to double the tax on cigarettes to pay for cuts in sales, property or income taxes, depending on what agreement he gets with legislators.

King, who was attending the Annual Conference of New England Governors and the Eastern Canadian Premiers, told Reuters he was confident the legislature would not be able to override his veto of another anti-smoking bill.
That bill also would have raised the tax per pack to 74 cents from 37 cents, but used the money to provide health insurance for needy children and prescription drugs for senior citizens.
The governor initially had proposed raising cigarette taxes to pay for income tax relief, but opened the door to other types of tax reductions in his new proposal.

"I've compromised and essentially put it into what's called in Maine the tax relief fund...And then my legislature and I will decide next year through the normal process how that fund will be dispersed, whether it's property tax, sales tax or income tax," he said. "And my guess is, based on the original bill that I vetoed, that there are not sufficient votes to override the veto."

The tax relief fund in March was set up by the legislature to absorb an approximately $30 million to $40 million budget surplus, which has surpassed forecasts because the economy has done better than predicted.
The state's fiscal year ends June 30.
"This is a fund that's designed to be sent back to the taxpayers. It's not determined in what form it will be sent." explained King.

Around five percent of the extra revenues that would be raised by doubling the state's cigarette taxes would help pay for an advertising campaign designed to prevent smoking. Maine has the highest rate of teenagers who smoke in the country, King noted, saying this had led to the consensus to raise the taxes on packs of cigarettes.
But he added that when childrens' health is looked at according to broader measures, the state appeared to be doing fairly well.
For example, a recent study put it second in the nation in terms of overall health, first in childhood immunization rates and third in death rates from infancy to 14 years of age.

"I don't want to come off as sounding like I say there's no problem, but what I'm saying is we're doing pretty well and that has to be weighed against what I consider the economic dstructiveness of increasing taxes."
He highlighted the state's high tax rates, saying he wanted to gradually reduce the net tax burden.

"Maine is the 10th highest tax state in the country and I don't think we can continue to raise taxes for whatever purpose, and if we want to do childrens' health or schools or whatever, we have to do it from within our existing means," he said. "And I'm not as governor going to approve a significant tax increase for any program."
